doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Bass solos: when to take them and when not
summary: Why bass solos can drain energy, his big band album with one solo, and learning to walk a solo like Hinton.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Did you ever wish that they would do the bass solo first, instead of all the sax players and everything, and you’ve been back there doing everything, and now be in the spotlight.

Well one of the issues is when it gets to the bass solo then everybody just kinds of goes away and nobody’s listening. There’s so many jokes and I know you’ve heard them, you know, about to get people to start talking again just give them a bass solo. But the thing is that sometimes it’s nice. Like I have an album that’s coming out in the fall, and it’s a big band thing of mine, but I only have one solo. And it’s mine. It’s mine. Just because I’m the leader of a group doesn’t mean that I’m going to solo on everything. But traditionally when you’re coming up, usually you have everybody playing 75 thousand choruses while

you’ve been supporting all that. And then there’s nobody to support you when you play. And that can be a drag sometimes. And so we try to — well either I’m saying, well I don’t want to solo. Because sometimes the bass solo tanks that energy that has been already established. So I don’t want to do that too. If I’m going to do it, I want to help make it go too. So it’s a decision sometimes, and my ego — I like to solo, I want to solo, and I think I play better solos than I used to. But most people don’t hire me to take solos. Ninety-nine percent of bass players, their job is to make the band swing and feel good. So I’ve never developed a solo. Some people think that’s all they want to do. And they actually, when they play they need a bass player to play for them. And it’s different styles of concepts and things, but how I learned how to play, the soloing was just — if they let me I was lucky, if they let me play. But I never thought about it. And sometimes they let me play and I’ll say no, this is not the time for a solo. And so now there are times where I’ve learned, well I’d like to solo on this tune. Then I can kind of orchestrate a little bit. But invariably they would always throw me towards something and it’s at a tempo I can’t play anyway, so I learn how to walk a solo, like Milt Hinton used to do, or some of the older players used to do. But then you’d go listen to Jimmy Blanton and he played great solos and it was long before I was even thought of, you know. So it’s all subjective.
